Issued at 158 AM CST Sun Nov 1 2026

It's a cloudy start to the day as weak shortwave energy works in 
aloft, with southerly winds at the surface keeping temperatures and 
dewpoints overnight above our average high for November 1st. It's 
those dewpoints that have been driving some fog out there. Central 
and northern MN have been on the cusp of fog all night and that will 
continue through about 10am. Outside of central MN, any brief 
clearings that develop quickly start to fill in with fog, but those 
clearings have been quickly filling back in with mid/upper clouds 
which has led to a bit of a whack-a-mole setup for fog overnight. 
Down in Iowa, we are seeing a patch of clearing skies down around 
Des Moines and most of the short term guidance and the NBM shows 
these lower cloud cover skies coming up into eastern MN and western 
WI later today. Given the fact that we will be starting the day with 
temepratures still in the 50s, we'll have no problem warming into 
the 60s. Depending on how much sun we get today, 925mb temps near 
15C will support highs in the low 70s, which is what the NBM 90th 
percentile has for highs for Mankato, Rochester, the Twin Cities, 
Eau Claire, and points in between.

Tonight, the longwave trough moving across the Rockies this morning 
will be heading out on to the Plains. Right now, this trough is 
becoming detached from the northern stream, with a southern stream 
jet streak being the feature that will push the trough out into the 
central CONUS. This southern stream jet streak will kick out into 
the Great Lakes tonight, leaving the longwave trough in a zone of 
weak upper flow until the next southern stream jet streak arrives 
midweek. Models are in good agreement through Monday night on the 
initial low pressure moving into central MN, but how this upper low 
and related surface low/s evolve the rest of the week is more 
uncertain. At the very least, we look to keep periods of rain 
showers going through Wednesday and possibly continuing into 
Thursday.

Where models maintain fairly good agreement is with the initial low 
that comes into central MN Monday night. This has shifted north some 
in the last 24 hours, but the idea of a large shield of moderate to 
heavy rain moving across the area during the day on Monday remains. 
Monday night, a dry slot will move into southern MN as this low 
becomes occluded. PWATs with this initial push of moisture will be 
near 1.6". The highest observed PWAT we've had in the month of 
November was 1.47" back with a 12z sounding on the 10th in 2022. 
Once this low hits the occlusion phase, models start to differ on 
how this and subsequent lows will evolve between MN/IA and WI 
through Thursday. As this system slowly churns across the area, 
we'll see periods of deformation rain come and go Tuesday and 
Wednesday. With this degree of moisture moving in, we continue to 
see some incredible QPF values for November, with storm totals over 
3" still possible from northeast SD into central MN, which would be 
more than twice our normal liquid precipitation for the entire month 
November.

By the end of the week, split flow will take shape as the broad 
trough moves into the Great Lakes. This will dry us out to end the 
week, but we may have one more shortwave to deal with on Saturday as 
a clipper type wave drops down out of Canada on its way around the 
eastern trough. Other than that though, the split flow looks to 
result in seasonably mild and dry weather into the middle of the 
month. For the winter fans out there wondering when we may finally 
start seeing snow and cold temperatures, you have to run out into 
the extended runs of the ECMWF and GFS to find any inkling of colder 
weather at the end of the month with our exceptionally mild fall 
weather continuing for the foreseeable future.
